transcript.text: my belling cooker keeps burnin stuff 1 day then next day its undercookd on same temp. been like it a cuple months. thermastat??

Inconsistent temperatures (burnt one day, undercooked the next at the same setting) are a classic sign of a faulty thermostat, so you're probably on the right track. A few other things can cause it, though, so it's worth checking before buying parts.

## Step 1: Confirm it with an oven thermometer (£5–10)
• Put it in the middle of the oven, set to 180°C, and wait about 20 minutes.
• Check it every few minutes for half an hour.
• Normal: it swings about ±10–15°C around 180.
• Faulty: it shoots way over (220+), sits well under, or behaves differently on different days.

Do this on a couple of separate days, since your problem is intermittent.

## Likely causes (most to least common)
1. Thermostat: the most common cause of erratic temperatures. On most Belling electric ovens it has a capillary tube and a sensor bulb clipped inside the oven cavity. Make sure the bulb hasn't come loose from its clips. If it's touching an element or hanging free, readings go haywire, and clipping it back is a free fix.
2. Fan oven element: if one coil is failing intermittently, you'll get undercooking on some days. You'd usually notice uneven cooking too.
3. Fan motor: if it's slow, noisy, or sometimes not spinning, heat won't circulate properly.
4. Door seal: if it's perished or loose, heat escapes. Check for gaps or hardened bits.
5. Selector switch / wiring: a loose or burnt connection can cause intermittent faults. Look for scorched terminals behind the back panel.

## Fixing it
• Find the model number (usually on a sticker around the door frame or on the back) so you get the right part. Belling thermostats are generally £20–50 online.
• Swapping a thermostat is a moderate DIY job: remove the back/side panels, unclip the sensor, and transfer the wires one at a time (take a photo first).
• ⚠️ Turn it off at the isolator switch/fuse box before opening any panels. Cookers run on a high-current circuit.
• If it's a gas oven, don't DIY it. Get a Gas Safe registered engineer.

If you're not confident, an appliance repair visit is typically £60–120 plus parts, which is often still cheaper than a new cooker.

Is it electric or gas, and is it a fan oven? I can point you to the specific part if you have the model number.

its electric, a belling 60cm double oven, main one is the fan one. i dont have a thermomiter tho and cant find the model label, think its hidden behind the drawer at the bottom. i make lasagne and cakes alot so its anoying lol

Since it's electric, this is doable yourself, and you can make progress without the model number or a thermometer.

## Finding the model label
• Behind the drawer: pull the bottom drawer fully out, then lift it up and towards you. Most come off their runners. The sticker is usually on the frame behind it.
• Other spots: the edges of the door frame (main or top oven), the inside of the drawer itself, or the back of the cooker.
• Paperwork: the manual or receipt, if you still have it.

You want the model number (e.g. something like "BFS60DO") and ideally the serial number too.

## Testing without a thermometer
Sugar test (free):
1. Put a teaspoon of plain white sugar on a bit of foil in the middle of the oven.
2. Set it to 180°C, let it preheat, then leave it 15 minutes. The sugar should stay white and grainy, since it melts at about 186°C.
3. Turn it up to 200°C for another 15 minutes. It should now melt and start to caramelise.

If it melts at 180, the oven's running hot. If it doesn't melt at 200, it's running cold. Try it on a couple of different days, since your problem comes and goes.

That said, a basic oven thermometer is only a few quid from most supermarkets or Amazon and is much more accurate, so it's worth grabbing one.

## Free checks to do first (oven off and cool)
• Thermostat sensor: look in the main oven, usually on the back wall near the fan cover, for a thin metal rod or bulb held in clips. If it's loose, dangling, or touching anything, clip it back. This is a common cause and costs nothing.
• Fan: with the oven on, does the fan always spin? Is it noisy, or does it sometimes stop?
• Element: the fan element is behind the back cover. If the oven struggles to heat on the "undercooked" days, the element may be failing.
• Door seal: check for gaps, tears, or loose corners.

## Useful clue: use the top oven
Cook the same thing in the top (non-fan) oven. If it comes out consistently fine, the fault is specific to the main oven's thermostat, fan, or element rather than the power supply or wiring.

## Meanwhile, for your lasagne and cakes
• Bake cakes in the top oven if they fit. Its conventional heat is actually great for cakes.
• Check things 10 minutes early, and use a skewer test for cakes.
• Cover lasagne with foil for most of the cook so it won't burn on a hot day, then uncover it for the last 10–15 minutes.

Once you've found the model number, I can help you track down the right thermostat. If you replace it yourself, switch the cooker off at the isolator switch first.

ok thanks, ill have a go at the sugar thing, sounds like when i do caramel for my trifle lol. the fan i think spins every time, i can hear it going. the door seal is a bit flattened at the top corner but the door shuts ok. still havnt found the label tho

Yes, it's basically the start of making caramel, so you'll know what you're looking for. You just don't want it going brown at 180°C.

## What your checks tell us
• Fan spinning every time probably rules out the fan motor. Note that the fan can spin fine even if the element behind it is failing, so the element isn't fully ruled out.
• Flattened seal corner is probably not the main culprit. A leaky seal makes an oven run cooler, but it wouldn't cause the burning days. To check it, close the door on a strip of paper at that corner and pull it out. If it slides out with no resistance, the seal's worth replacing eventually (usually £10–20 and it just clips in), but it's not urgent.
• Burnt one day, undercooked the next still points most strongly at the thermostat, since it's the one part that can go wrong in both directions.

## More places to look for the label
• Drawer: pull it fully out, then lift the front up and pull. It should unhook from the runners. The label is often on the floor or front frame behind it.
• Door frames: open each oven door and check the edges of the frame around the opening, including the top oven and grill compartment.
• The door itself: check the side edges of each door.
• Back of the cooker: if you can pull it out safely, there's often a rating plate there too.

If you still can't find it, Belling's customer service can often identify the model from photos of the front and controls. Once you have the model number, the thermostat is an easy part to find.

Let me know how the sugar test goes. If it melts at 180°C on one day and won't melt at 200°C on another, that pretty much confirms the thermostat.
